questions.q: Why does storage_client.storage_accounts.begin_create() return a poller instead of the finished storage account?
options: Creating a storage account takes real time on Azure's side, so the SDK returns immediately and poller.result() blocks until it's actually done
begin_create never actually creates anything on its own
It returns a poller only when the request fails
Poller objects are required by every Python function regardless of what they do
questions.explain: begin_create starts an asynchronous, long-running operation and hands back a poller right away; calling .result() is what waits for completion.

questions.q: Why is calling resource_groups.create_or_update() before creating the storage account safe to run more than once?
options: It only works the very first time a script is ever run
It's idempotent — rerunning it against a resource group that already exists doesn't fail or duplicate anything
It deletes and recreates the resource group every single time
Azure blocks any script that calls it more than once
questions.explain: create_or_update is idempotent, tying directly back to Chapter 1's lesson on why a script should be safe to rerun.

questions.q: In the Boto3 S3 example, what does CreateBucketConfiguration with LocationConstraint do?
options: It permanently deletes any existing bucket with the same name
It has no real effect on how create_bucket behaves
It's required by create_bucket for every AWS region except us-east-1, or the call raises an error
It is required in every AWS region including us-east-1
questions.explain: This is the one real regional gotcha with S3's create_bucket call — omit it outside us-east-1 and the call fails.

questions.q: Why does the Boto3 example wrap create_bucket in try/except ClientError?
options: It follows Chapter 1's error-handling lesson, catching a real AWS error instead of letting the script crash
try/except is required syntax for every single Python function call
It prevents the bucket from ever actually being created
ClientError is unrelated to AWS and only applies to Azure scripts
questions.explain: ClientError is boto3's real exception type for failed AWS API calls, and catching it matches the error-handling practice from Chapter 1.

questions.q: What does this lesson's script demonstrate by combining Lessons 9 through 11?
options: That PowerShell is required even when using the Azure SDK for Python
That Python cannot actually be used to create real cloud resources
The official SDK, the shared client pattern, and the credential chain all working together to provision one real resource
That credentials must always be hardcoded for the script to function
questions.explain: This lesson is the payoff of the chapter — the SDK, the client pattern, and the credential chain all shown working together in one real, runnable script.
